identity.title: Abdominojugular (hepatojugular) reflux: sustained JVP rise >3 cm with 10-30 s abdominal pressure

technique.how: With the top of the JVP column visible and the patient breathing quietly through an open mouth (no Valsalva), apply firm steady mid-abdominal pressure with the flat hand for 10 s (Ewy) up to 30 s while watching the neck veins. Positive = a sustained rise >3 cm (or >=4 cm / 3 mmHg) lasting through compression, dropping abruptly on release.
technique.prerequisites: Visible JVP baseline; patient able to breathe quietly through an open mouth; no acute abdominal pain.
technique.contraindications: Painful or surgical abdomen, recent abdominal surgery, known AAA; do not perform during a Valsalva.

interpretation.positive_finding: A sustained rise indicates the right heart cannot accommodate the increased venous return, which in the absence of isolated RV failure reflects elevated left-sided filling pressure (PCWP >=15 mmHg). In chronic HF patients a positive test corresponds to a mean wedge pressure near 19 mmHg vs 10.5 mmHg when negative.
interpretation.negative_finding: A transient rise that falls within a few seconds is normal (column rises <3 cm). A negative test lowers but does not exclude elevated filling pressures, particularly in acute dyspnea where sensitivity is limited.
interpretation.pitfalls: Straining or breath-holding produces a false-positive rise; too little pressure or too short a compression produces a false negative. Isolated RV failure (RV infarction), tricuspid regurgitation and constriction give a positive test without left-sided congestion.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive AJR supports a cardiac (elevated filling pressure) cause of dyspnea/edema and favors diuresis; negative AJR with flat JVP argues against congestion.

sources.citation: Butman SM, Ewy GA, Standen JR, Kern KB, Hahn E. Bedside cardiovascular examination in patients with severe chronic heart failure: importance of rest or inducible jugular venous distension. J Am Coll Cardiol 1993;22(4):968-74.
Ducas J, Magder S, McGregor M. Validity of the hepatojugular reflux as a clinical test for congestive heart failure. Am J Cardiol 1983;52(10):1299-303.
Ewy GA. The abdominojugular test: technique and hemodynamic correlates. Ann Intern Med 1988;109(6):456-60.
Wang CS, FitzGerald JM, Schulzer M, Mak E, Ayas NT. Does this dyspneic patient in the emergency department have congestive heart failure? JAMA 2005;294(15):1944-56.
Cook DJ, Simel DL. The Rational Clinical Examination. Does this patient have abnormal central venous pressure? JAMA 1996;275(8):630-4.
Mueller C, Frana B, Scholer A, Laule-Kilian K, Perruchoud AP. Emergency diagnosis of congestive heart failure: impact of signs and symptoms. Can J Cardiol 2005;21(11):921-4.

estimates.target_condition: Elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (>=18 mmHg)
estimates.population: 52 patients with severe chronic heart failure undergoing in-hospital transplant evaluation; index finding = jugular venous distension at rest OR inducible by the abdominojugular test
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.81/(1-0.80) = 4.05; LR- = (1-0.81)/0.80 = 0.24 from reported sensitivity 81% and specificity 80% (CIs not reported in abstract)
estimates.quote: had the best combination of sensitivity (81%), specificity (80%) and predictive accuracy (81%) for elevation of the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure

estimates.target_condition: Impaired resting cardiac function / congestive heart failure (CVP rise >=3 mmHg with abdominal compression)
estimates.population: Catheterized patients with impaired (n=19) vs normal resting cardiac function; CVP measured directly during standardized abdominal compression
estimates.reference_standard: Direct central venous pressure measurement during abdominal compression, with cardiac function classified clinically/hemodynamically
estimates.computed_from: Sensitivity = 16/19 = 0.84; specificity not computable because the abstract states no normal-function patient rose >2 mmHg but does not give that group's n
estimates.quote: In 16 of 19 patients with impaired function, CVP increased by greater than or equal to 3 mm Hg.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not perform on a tender or surgical abdomen or when the baseline JVP top cannot be seen (the test requires a visible column to judge the change).
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Positive AJR with hypotension and clear lungs should prompt urgent evaluation for RV infarction, tamponade or PE rather than empiric diuresis.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Reproducibility depends on standardized pressure and timing (Ewy 1988); untrained examiners often press too briefly or let the patient Valsalva.

extraction_notes: Wang 2005 RCE lists AJR LR+ ~6.4 with a wide CI in its table; JAMA full text not accessible via tool so not entered. Ewy 1988 (Ann Intern Med) gives hemodynamic correlates (mean PCWP 19 vs 10.5 mmHg; positive test suggests PCWP >=15) but no sens/spec in the abstract, so it is cited for technique/threshold only. Butman 1993's index finding is JVD at rest OR AJR-inducible, entered with that label. Ducas 1983 sensitivity computed from 16/19; specificity left null (denominator for normal-function group not in abstract). Mueller 2005 reports OR 2.7 for HJR in ED dyspnea (not an LR); cited without estimate. Status partially_quantified because no estimate isolates the AJR alone with both sens and spec.
